analysis.one_liner: Caps compensation in medical malpractice lawsuits and makes it harder for injured patients to sue health providers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 16 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for medical malpractice lawsuits nationwide. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, make it harder to win punitive damages, cut the share of winnings lawyers can collect, shorten the deadlines for filing claims, and reduce awards by any insurance benefits the patient already received. Supporters argued it would lower doctors' insurance costs and defensive medicine; critics said it would mainly shield insurers and providers from paying injured patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care providers and hospitals gain protection from large jury awards, and the medical liability insurance industry gains from federal caps that reduce the payouts it must cover. Both would pay lower malpractice premiums.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated purpose is to lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce defensive medicine in order to improve patient access to care, while leaving full recovery of all economic damages (medical bills, lost earnings) uncapped.
It caps attorney contingency fees on a sliding scale, so in large settlements a bigger share of the recovery would reach the patient rather than the lawyer.
It requires sanctions, including payment of the other side's legal costs, against lawyers who file frivolous malpractice suits.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence, especially children, seniors, and stay-at-home spouses whose injuries produce little "economic" loss; they would bear the cost of capped compensation and shortened filing deadlines. Plaintiffs' attorneys also lose through fee caps.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages (pain, suffering, disfigurement, loss of companionship) would fall hardest on patients whose injuries carry little provable financial loss, such as children, retirees, and stay-at-home spouses, while doing nothing to limit awards for lost wages and medical bills.

Punitive damages would be allowed only for malicious intent or deliberate disregard proven by clear and convincing evidence, capped at the greater of twice economic damages or $250,000, and the jury would not be told about the cap, sharply limiting punishment for the worst cases of negligence.

Awards would be reduced by any collateral source benefits such as health insurance or disability payments the patient is entitled to, meaning privately purchased insurance could be counted against the patient's recovery.
The bill would override state jury systems and damage rules in malpractice cases, pre-empting state law wherever state rules give plaintiffs more.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains the bill promises ordinary people (lower premiums, less defensive medicine, faster resolution of claims) are indirect and disputed, while the costs are direct and certain: injured patients would lose compensation, lose part of their insurance-funded recovery, face shorter filing deadlines, and pay punitive-damage standards that make the worst cases nearly impossible to punish. The bill leaves economic damages uncapped, which softens the blow for high earners, but the overall design shifts risk away from insurers and providers and onto the people least able to bear it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 10, 2007, by Senator Ensign along with 14 other Senate Republicans and was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
It carried 16 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no Democratic support.
The committee took no further action on the bill for the remainder of the 110th Congress; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical liability insurers, hospitals, and physicians kept the existing malpractice rules, which allow larger jury awards than the bill would have permitted. State-level jury verdicts and patients' full damage rights under state law were left untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Malpractice insurers and providers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Senate Republicans, and the bill never gained a Democratic sponsor or a committee hearing in a Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The bill's central beneficiaries would be the insurers that write malpractice policies: damage caps, tougher punitive-damage standards, and collateral-source offsets all reduce the payouts insurers must cover and would support lower premiums.

Providers and hospital systems would gain protection from large verdicts, including joint liability limits and shielding from suits over FDA-approved drugs and devices they prescribe. The bill's stated rationale is lower malpractice costs for them, not compensation for patients.

The bill caps plaintiff attorney contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% of large recoveries) and requires sanctions for frivolous filings, cutting into the trial bar's revenue. Their financial interest runs opposite to insurers' in this bill.

Section 8 bars naming a health care provider as a party in product liability or class action suits over FDA-approved drugs, biologics, and devices used as approved, insulating prescribing providers and reducing one avenue of pressure on manufacturers.
